title: Le Corbusier
objective: After this level you can explain the idea of a house as a machine for living in.
summary: Le Corbusier called a house a machine for living in. His Dom-ino frame freed walls, leading to five points: pilotis, roof garden, free plan, long windows, free facade, shown in the Villa Savoye.

cards.headline: In 1923, Le Corbusier wrote that a house is a machine for living in.
cards.body: The line comes from his book Vers une architecture: "La maison est une machine à habiter." It sounds cold. He meant that a house should first serve the body, giving comfort as efficiently as a good machine. Only then, he said, does it become a place for meditation and for beauty. So what does a living machine look like?

cards.headline: Dom-ino: a house as a kit
cards.body: In 1914 he drew the Dom-ino system: three concrete floor slabs, six posts and a staircase. That's the whole thing. As in Level 8's frame, the skeleton carries the floors, so no wall has to hold anything up. Walls can go anywhere, windows can run the full length of the front, and the module can be repeated again and again. The rest of his career grew out of this kit.

cards.headline: Five points, and a garage built to fit the car
cards.body: In 1927 he set out five points for a new architecture: pilotis (posts that lift the house off the ground), a roof garden, a free plan, long horizontal windows and a free facade. Every one follows from the frame. The Villa Savoye at Poissy, France, built from 1928 to 1931, shows them best. Its ground floor even curves to match the turning radius of the family car, which drove in under the pilotis. A machine for living, with the car's needs designed right in.

mascot.line: Most houses fit the car into the design. This design was shaped around the car.

cards.fact: Seventeen of Le Corbusier's works are World Heritage.
cards.context: UNESCO listed them together in 2016, spread across seven countries. Seven countries, one architect, one listing.

questions.prompt: Which of these is one of Le Corbusier's five points for a new architecture?

options.label: Thick load-bearing outer walls
options.rationale: The five points depend on walls carrying nothing.

options.label: A steep pitched roof
options.rationale: His fifth point puts a garden on a flat roof.

options.label: Small, deep-set windows
options.rationale: He called for long horizontal windows.

questions.explanation: The five points are pilotis, a roof garden, a free plan, long horizontal windows and a free facade.

questions.prompt: How does the Villa Savoye's curved ground floor show Le Corbusier's 'machine for living' idea?

options.label: It hides the machinery that heats the house
options.rationale: The curve is about the car.

options.label: It matches the turning radius of the family car
It makes the house look like a ship
options.rationale: The curve follows the car's path.

options.label: It keeps rain away from the pilotis
options.rationale: It was shaped for the car driving under the house.

questions.explanation: The ground floor curves to fit the car's turning radius as it drove in under the pilotis: the house built around how it would be used.

questions.prompt: Level 8 split the jobs of wall and frame. In Le Corbusier's Dom-ino system, what carries the floors?

options.label: Thick walls of brick around the edge
options.rationale: The Dom-ino has no load-bearing walls.

options.label: Cables hung from a roof truss
The glass of the windows
options.rationale: Walls and windows carry nothing in a frame.
